claims.claim: Gordon opens her study by asserting that Wolfe writes elegant and evocative prose.
claims.source: Joan Gordon, Gene Wolfe (Starmont Reader's Guide 29, Starmont House, 1986)
claims.quote: elegant and evocative prose

claims.claim: Gordon says Wolfe's stories differ from most other science fiction in their emphasis on ambiguity.
claims.source: Joan Gordon, Gene Wolfe (Starmont Reader's Guide 29, Starmont House, 1986)
claims.quote: their emphasis on ambiguity

claims.claim: Gordon writes that Wolfe seldom stresses action in his fiction.
claims.source: Joan Gordon, Gene Wolfe (Starmont Reader's Guide 29, Starmont House, 1986)
claims.quote: Wolfe seldom stresses action or

claims.claim: Gordon says Wolfe typically relates his sociological stories in a flat, business-like tone that mimics the callous language of bureaucratic management.
claims.source: Joan Gordon, Gene Wolfe (Starmont Reader's Guide 29, Starmont House, 1986)
claims.quote: business-like tone that mimics the callous

claims.claim: Gordon says that in his most characteristic fiction Wolfe adopts a cool tone.
claims.source: Joan Gordon, Gene Wolfe (Starmont Reader's Guide 29, Starmont House, 1986)
claims.quote: Wolfe adopts a cool tone

claims.claim: Gordon says the sentence structure of The Book of the New Sun works not to obfuscate but to illustrate.
claims.source: Joan Gordon, Gene Wolfe (Starmont Reader's Guide 29, Starmont House, 1986)
claims.quote: its language does, not to obfuscate but to

claims.claim: Gordon measures the opening paragraph of The Shadow of the Torturer and reports that its first sentence is eleven words long.
claims.source: Joan Gordon, Gene Wolfe (Starmont Reader's Guide 29, Starmont House, 1986)
claims.quote: the first sentence is fairly short (eleven words)

claims.claim: Gordon reports the two remaining sentences of that opening paragraph as thirty-two words and twenty-seven words.
claims.source: Joan Gordon, Gene Wolfe (Starmont Reader's Guide 29, Starmont House, 1986)
claims.quote: (thirty—two words and twenty—seven words)

claims.claim: Gordon quotes Wolfe's appendix to The Shadow of the Torturer saying his substituted words are intended to be suggestive rather than definitive.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, appendix to The Shadow of the Torturer, quoted in Joan Gordon, Gene Wolfe (Starmont Reader's Guide 29, Starmont House, 1986)
claims.quote: suggestive rather than definitive
claims.page: ch. VIII, p. 75, quoting ST Appendix p. 302

claims.claim: Gordon quotes Wolfe saying he found a writer's assumption of a single uniform culture covering a whole world both incredible and boring.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, 'Helioscope' in The Castle of the Otter, quoted in Joan Gordon, Gene Wolfe (Starmont Reader's Guide 29, Starmont House, 1986)
claims.quote: both incredible and boring
claims.page: ch. VIII, p. 80, quoting CO pp. 8-9

claims.claim: Gordon says the Commonwealth of The Book of the New Sun has a caste system in which each caste has its own culture.
claims.source: Joan Gordon, Gene Wolfe (Starmont Reader's Guide 29, Starmont House, 1986)
claims.quote: each caste with its own culture

claims.claim: Gordon argues that setting in the tetralogy confirms style and directs the reader to theme.
claims.source: Joan Gordon, Gene Wolfe (Starmont Reader's Guide 29, Starmont House, 1986)
claims.quote: setting confirms style and directs us to

claims.claim: Gordon calls Wolfe's tendency to raise rather than answer questions one source of his evocative power.
claims.source: Joan Gordon, Gene Wolfe (Starmont Reader's Guide 29, Starmont House, 1986)
claims.quote: tendency to raise rather than answer

claims.claim: Gordon describes the myth John Marsch constructs in the second novella of The Fifth Head of Cerberus as the simulated artifact of a culture whose existence has left little trace.
claims.source: Joan Gordon, Gene Wolfe (Starmont Reader's Guide 29, Starmont House, 1986)
claims.quote: The myth is the simulated artifact of a culture

claims.claim: Gordon says the memoir-with-embedded-stories form of Peace distances the narrator from his material.
claims.source: Joan Gordon, Gene Wolfe (Starmont Reader's Guide 29, Starmont House, 1986)
claims.quote: distances the narrator from his material

claims.feature: other: didactic register suppresses the device
claims.claim: Gordon says that in Operation ARES the didactic purpose is so clear that ambiguity and an invitation to interpret have no place.
claims.source: Joan Gordon, Gene Wolfe (Starmont Reader's Guide 29, Starmont House, 1986)
claims.quote: an invitation to interpret have no place

claims.claim: Gordon gives the length of the four volumes of The Book of the New Sun as 1222 pages in the first editions.
claims.source: Joan Gordon, Gene Wolfe (Starmont Reader's Guide 29, Starmont House, 1986)
claims.quote: 1222 pages in the first editions

claims.claim: Attebery calls Wolfe a writer with a love of indirection and ambiguity equal to Henry James's.
claims.source: Brian Attebery, Strategies of Fantasy (Indiana University Press, 1992), ch. 7 'Science Fantasy'
claims.quote: an equal love of indirection and ambiguity

claims.claim: Attebery says Wolfe introduces the new and strange by using words that are old and strange.
claims.source: Brian Attebery, Strategies of Fantasy (Indiana University Press, 1992), ch. 7 'Science Fantasy'
claims.quote: He introduces the new and strange by

claims.claim: Attebery describes Wolfe's archaic half-familiar words - fuligin, lazaret, hierodule, pelerine - as mostly Latinate.
claims.source: Brian Attebery, Strategies of Fantasy (Indiana University Press, 1992), ch. 7 'Science Fantasy'
claims.quote: fuligin, lazaret, hierodule, and pelerine

claims.claim: Attebery says Wolfe generally invents by reusing what is forgotten rather than by coining.
claims.source: Brian Attebery, Strategies of Fantasy (Indiana University Press, 1992), ch. 7 'Science Fantasy'
claims.quote: Wolfe generally invents by reusing

claims.claim: Andre-Driussi reports Wolfe denying that the Lexicon's entries were guesses, saying instead that Andre-Driussi looks things up.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, reported in 'Tell me about the Lexicon Urthus': an interview with Michael Andre-Driussi, Ultan's Library, 2008
claims.quote: No, not at all – he looks things up!
claims.page: interview, reply on the 1991 World Fantasy Convention

claims.claim: The Ultan's Library interviewer describes one of Wolfe's naming schemes in the Urth Cycle as naming people in the Commonwealth after Catholic saints.
claims.source: Ultan's Library (interviewer), interview with Michael Andre-Driussi, 2008
claims.quote: naming people in the Commonwealth after Catholic saints

claims.claim: Andre-Driussi says one of the Lexicon's special articles is a history that puts all the posthistorical bits of the Urth Cycle into one place.
claims.source: Michael Andre-Driussi, interview in Ultan's Library, 2008
claims.quote: putting together all the posthistorical bits into one place

claims.claim: Andre-Driussi says it took him eight years to sell all 1,000 copies of the first edition of Lexicon Urthus.
claims.source: Michael Andre-Driussi, interview in Ultan's Library, 2008
claims.quote: it took me eight years to sell all 1,000 copies!

claims.claim: Joan Gordon divides Wolfe criticism into macro and micro kinds and places her own work on the macro side.
claims.source: Joan Gordon, 'Micro-Wolfenomics', Ultan's Library, 2020
claims.quote: There are two kinds of Wolfeian criticism: macro and micro

claims.claim: Joan Gordon confirms in 2020 that her 1986 Starmont Reader's Guide proposed that the whole of Peace unspools from Weer taking the Thematic Apperception Test.
claims.source: Joan Gordon, 'Micro-Wolfenomics', Ultan's Library, 2020
claims.quote: the whole novel unspools from Weer
